C45225.observed: What was checked: what the chip under the row is labelled with when the whole quantity comes out of one bin. What happened: the chip carries the bin's own name - "Unassigned" for the part tried, and other parts on this system sit in bins named "D1B" and "SHOP" - so the technician reads the place, not a code or a count.
C45225.not_observed: The other half of this case - that a quantity split across two or more bins is labelled "N bins" instead - could not be seen: every stocked part on this branch sits in a single bin, so no split can be made.

C45228.observed: What was checked: whether you are allowed to take more of a part than the bin actually holds - which a shop sometimes has to do - and whether the system merely warns or actually blocks you. What happened: a part whose bin holds 6 was asked for with a quantity of 99. The row warned about it in plain words but did not stop anything: Save went through and the part was added. So the bin is allowed to go negative, and the decision is left with the person doing the work.

C45229.observed: What was checked: whether the user is told clearly, and visibly, when the bin they are pulling from does not hold enough. What happened: with a bin holding 6 and a quantity of 99 entered, the note beside the chip read exactly "Only 6 here. Pulling 99 takes this bin negative." - naming both numbers so there is no guessing - and both the note and the bin chip itself were shown in orange warning colouring rather than the usual blue, so it catches the eye without blocking the work.
